entities.summary:
Sangiban was the Alan king at the time of Attila's invasion of Gaul (451) and successor of Goar as king of the Alan foederati settled in the region around Aurelianum. The Romans and Visigoths had suspected Sangiban of betraying them, so they placed him at the center of their line opposing the Huns. This led to the Alans bearing the main force against the Huns, ultimately contributing to the defeat of Attila's invasion.

Sangiban is best known for his role in the Battle of Châlons, where he had promised Attila before the battle to open the city gates and deliver Aurelianum to the Huns. However, the Romans and Visigoths suspected this betrayal and placed Sangiban at the center of their line, preventing him from defecting.

The legacy of Sangiban's actions can be seen in the aftermath of Attila's defeat, as the Alans continued to play a significant role in European politics for centuries. The Battle of Châlons marked an important turning point in the history of the Western Roman Empire and had far-reaching consequences for the development of European society.

In recent years, historians have sought to reevaluate Sangiban's place in the narrative of Attila's invasion, highlighting the complexities of Alan-Alan relations and the role of the Alans as a buffer state between Rome and the Huns.
